patches.new: We need two experimental facts from the early twentieth century. We take them on trust; HRW \cite{hrw} describes the experiments in its chapters on photons and matter waves. First, Planck (1900) and Einstein (1905) concluded that light of frequency $f$ exchanges energy with matter only in packets, called photons, of energy $E=hf$. Einstein was explaining the photoelectric effect, in which light knocks electrons out of a metal. Here $h=6.62607015\times10^{-34}$~J\,s is Planck's constant. Second, Compton's 1923 experiments, scattering X-rays from electrons, showed that each photon also carries momentum $p=h/\lambda$, with $\lambda$ the wavelength of the light.

If a measurement of position is repeated on many identically prepared particles, the average result is the probability-weighted average of $x$ (an average weighted by $\abs\Psi^2$, like the center of mass of a rod with linear density $\abs\Psi^2$):
patches.new:
First, a fact about averages. Suppose a measurement has possible outcomes $x_1,x_2,\dots$. In many repeated trials, outcome $x_i$ occurs a fraction $P_i$ of the time, its probability, so $\sum_iP_i=1$. In $N_{\rm tr}$ trials, outcome $x_i$ occurs $P_iN_{\rm tr}$ times. The plain average of all results is therefore
\[
\frac{1}{N_{\rm tr}}\sum_i(P_iN_{\rm tr})\,x_i=\sum_iP_ix_i,
\]
which is each outcome weighted by its probability. Now apply this to position. Slice the line into thin slices of width $\dd x$. By the Born rule the slice at $x$ has probability $\abs\Psi^2\dd x$, and in the limit of thin slices the sum over slices becomes an integral. So if a measurement of position is repeated on many identically prepared particles, the average result is the probability-weighted average of $x$ (an average weighted by $\abs\Psi^2$, like the center of mass of a rod with linear density $\abs\Psi^2$):

patches.old: Applied to orthonormal eigenfunctions, Eq.~\eqref{eq:schrodinger-hermitian-def} says $\bra mQ\ket n=\bra nQ\ket m^*$, which is the matrix condition $Q_{mn}=Q_{nm}^*$.
patches.new:
Apply Eq.~\eqref{eq:schrodinger-hermitian-def} to any two allowed functions $\psi_m,\psi_n$, for example members of an orthonormal basis. Then
\[
\bra mQ\ket n=\int(Q\psi_m)^*\psi_n\,\dd x=\left(\int\psi_n^*\,Q\psi_m\,\dd x\right)^*=\bra nQ\ket m^*,
\]
where the middle step uses $(ab)^*=a^*b^*$ inside the integral. This is the matrix condition $Q_{mn}=Q_{nm}^*$.
